And the fact that "he said this concerning the temple of his body" the Jews, hindered by their malice, misheard and understood concerning that temple of stone,

which is manifest from the fact that, answering, they said: "In forty and six years was this temple built, and dost thou raise it up in three days?" And consider that not one false witness came forward for this testimony (for one was not sufficient for those wishing to kill Jesus, since the law commanded: "One witness shall not stand to give testimony against a man"), but neither were there three; for though many false witnesses came forward, scarcely two were found who seemed to say anything. But neither were their testimonies in agreement, as Mark sets forth; for he says in this manner, that "the chief priests and the whole council sought testimony against Jesus, that they might deliver him to death, and found none; for many spoke false testimony against him, and their testimonies were not in agreement. And others rising up spoke false testimony against him: that we heard him saying: that I destroy this temple made with hands, and in three days I will make another not made with hands. But neither so were their testimonies in agreement". For a testimony is in agreement when they say the same things, but they are not in agreement when they are dissonant with one another, such as were the testimonies of these who were bringing forward testimonies against Jesus. And if Matthew and Mark speak the truth (which we ought to believe), let us attempt to show how not even the testimonies of these two themselves were in agreement, since they did not bring forward the same things. For according to Matthew they said: This man said: I am able to destroy the temple of God and in three days to rebuild it, but according to Mark: "That we heard him saying: that I destroy this temple made with hands, and in three days I will rebuild another not made with hands". Whether therefore, saying these things twice, since they did not say the same things, their testimonies were not found in agreement with one another; or whether the one said what Matthew sets forth, and the other what Mark wrote, and thereby "their testimonies were not in agreement" with one another.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
And the chief priest, rising up, said to him: Do you answer nothing to the things which these men testify against you? But Jesus was silent (26, 62. 63a).

In these events one may understand as fulfilled the prophecy which says: "while the sinner stood against me, I was made dumb and was humbled and kept silent from good things", so that that sinner foretold in these words may be understood to be Caiaphas, who stood against Jesus. At the same time we learn also from this passage to despise the voices of slanderers and false witnesses, so that we neither hold them worthy of our reply, nor defend our own selves where the things said against us are not consistent. For what need is there to resist those who resist themselves by saying things contrary to themselves? Especially where it is a greater thing freely and bravely to be silent than to defend oneself without any profit, so that we may not be humbled by false witnesses and wicked slanderers.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
This place teaches us to contemn the clamours of slanderers and false witnesses, and not to consider those who speak unbeseeming things of us worthy of an answer; but then, above all, when it is greater to be manfully and resolutely silent, than to plead our cause in vain.

Under the Law, we do indeed find many instances of this adjuration (Numb. 5:19, 1 Kings 22:16.); but I judge that a man who would live according to the Gospel should not adjure another; for if we are not permitted to swear, surely not to adjure. But he that regards Jesus commanding the daemons, and giving His disciples power over them, will say, that to address the daemons by the power given by the Saviour, is not to adjure them. But the High Priest did sin in laying a snare for Jesus; imitating his father, who twice asked the Saviour, If thou be Christ the Son of God. (Matt. 4.) Hence one might rightly say, that to doubt concerning the Son of God, whether Christ be He, is the work of the Devil.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
And the chief priest said to him: I adjure you by the living God, that you tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God. And Jesus said to him: You have said it (26, 63ᵇ. 64ᵃ).

And indeed in the Law we find the practice of adjuring used on several occasions. For in Numbers the Law says that "the priest shall adjure her" (that is, that woman in whose husband there has arisen "a spirit of jealousy"), "and shall say to the woman" (this is, the priest): "if no one has lain with you, and unless you have transgressed so as to be defiled by a man not your own, you shall be innocent of this cursed water of accusation". And after a few words: "and the priest", he says, "shall adjure the woman with the adjurations of this curse". Likewise in the third book of Kingdoms king Ahab says to Micaiah: "Yet twice more do I adjure you, that you speak to me the truth in the name of the Lord". Now the king adjured the prophet, and he adjured not as the priest in Numbers; for the latter did so from the precept of the Law, but the former of his own choice. And now in the present passage the priest adjures Jesus by the living God. But I judge that it is not fitting for a man who wishes to live according to the Gospel to adjure another. For it is similar to what the Lord himself says in the Gospel: "But I say, not to swear at all" and not to adjure at all;

for if it is not permitted to swear, so far as concerns the evangelical commandment of Christ, it is true that neither is it permitted to adjure another.

Therefore it is manifest that the chief priest unlawfully adjured Jesus, although he may seem to have adjured him by the living God.

Someone will ask whether it is fitting even to adjure demons. And he who looks to the many who have dared to do such things will say that this is not done without reason; but he who looks to Jesus … commanding the demons, but also giving power to his disciples over all demons

and to heal infirmities, will say that to adjure demons is not according to the power given by the Savior: for it is a Jewish practice. This (even if sometimes something of the kind is done by our own people) is similar to that whereby demons are wont to be adjured by the adjurations written by Solomon. But those very people who use those adjurations sometimes do not even use properly established books, and with certain adjurations received even from the Hebrew they adjure the demons.

Nevertheless it was not fitting for our Lord to answer the adjuration of the chief priest, as though he had suffered compulsion from the one adjuring against his own will. For which reason he neither denied that he was the Christ, the Son of God, nor openly confessed it, but as though taking the very one adjuring him as witness (since it is he himself who in the priest's questioning was pronounced the Christ, the Son of God), saying: You have said it.

And since "everyone who commits sin is born of the devil", and the chief priest was committing sin by plotting against Jesus, therefore he was born of the devil, and as one born of the devil he was imitating his own father, who twice, in doubt, questions the Savior: "if you are the Son of God", as is written in his temptations; for "if you are the Son of God" and if you are the Christ, the Son of God are alike. For in this passage one may rightly say that to doubt concerning the Son of God whether he himself be the Christ is the work of the devil and of the chief priest plotting against our Lord. But Peter was not found to be such; for without any doubt he pronounced: "you are the Christ, the Son of the living God", nor did he there place if. For which reason he was called "blessed", because "not flesh and blood" had revealed it to him, "but God the Father who is in heaven". But those who say with doubt: "if you are the Son of God", are strangers to all blessedness. For because that chief priest was not worthy of the teaching of Christ, therefore he does not teach him, nor say, "I am", but taking the word of his own mouth he turns it into a refutation of him, saying: You have said it, so that in this way he might seem to be refuted, not taught.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: It was not fit that the Lord should answer the High Priest's adjuration as though under compulsion, wherefore He neither denied nor confessed Himself to be the Son of God. For he was not worthy to be the object of Christ's teaching, therefore He does not instruct him, but taking up his own words retorts them upon him. This sitting of the Son of Man seems to me to denote a certain regal security; by the power of God, Who is the only power, is He securely seated to Whom is given by His Father all power in heaven as in earth. And there will come a time when the enemies shall see this establishment. Indeed this has begun to be fulfilled from the earliest time of the dispensation; for the disciples saw Him rising from the dead, and thereby saw Him seated on the right hand of power. Or, In respect of that eternity of duration which is with God, from the beginning of the world to the end of it is but one day; it is therefore no wonder that the Saviour here says, Shortly, signifying that there is but short time before the end come. He prophesies moreover, that they should not only see Him sitting at the right hand of power, but also coming in the clouds of heaven. These clouds are the Prophets and Apostles, whom He commands to rain when it is required, they are the clouds that pass not away, but bearing the image of the heavenly, (1 Cor. 15:49.) are worthy to be the throne of God, as heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ. (Rom. 8:17.)

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Yet I say to you: from now on you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the Power, and coming upon the clouds of heaven (26, 64ᵇ).

Since it is not written at the right hand of God, but in all the evangelists at the right hand of the Power (and "of God" is not added), it is worthwhile to discern what it is for the Son of Man to sit at the right hand of the Power. Likewise the three evangelists write similarly: you shall see him sitting; and to the simple, indeed, who can hear nothing lofty in that which he says sitting, it is granted to understand it as if he said "established above the Power." But to those to whom it is possible to search out all things by the Spirit, "even the depths of God," they will understand both what is written: "you who sit upon the cherubim, appear" and: "I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up" and: "the Lord said to my Lord: sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet" and other things of the like. These things that are said of God sitting are likewise also said of Christ. And these ought to be compared with the present saying, so that from a lowly and fabulous estimation we may see what the sitting of Christ signifies after the manner of men. But it seems to me that the sitting of the Son of Man signifies a certain foundation and royal steadfastness. According to the Power, therefore — he who alone is the Power and is properly so named — he is also established at the right hand, he who has received all power from the Father, as "in heaven and on earth"; and this foundation even the adversaries will one day see, after the blessed have with joy seen him.

But according to Mark it does not have from now on, but purely, that is: "you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the Power"; and according to him there will be nothing contrary to the things we have handed down. But according to Matthew, who says from now on you shall see, and according to Luke, who says "from this time the Son of Man will be" and the rest, it must be inquired whether, from the time the Savior said these things, they were fulfilled also in those who heard what he said: from now on you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the Power. And we say that it can be seen as fulfilled, since from that time, that is, from the time of the dispensation, the Son of Man sat at the right hand of the Power, and his disciples saw him rising from the dead, and through this they saw him established at the right hand of the Power, according to what we have handed down above. Or thus: see whether you can measure the hour and the day not according to the brevity of hours and days that is among men, but according to the length that is with the eternal Lord, to whom from the foundation of the world until its consummation there is one day — which is demonstrated by the parable, where he speaks of those hired into the vineyard in the morning and at the third hour and the sixth and up to the eleventh. It is therefore no wonder that here the Savior says that from now on until then there is a very short span, in which span he was saying: you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the Power to those who were then hearing him — perhaps then when "the Lord said to my Lord: sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet", among whom were also those to whom he was saying from now on you shall see; for Caiaphas too was an enemy, who was plotting against Christ.

And he was prophesying that these would see him not only sitting at the right hand of the Power, but also would see him coming (as Matthew indeed says) upon the clouds of heaven. But what are the clouds upon which he will come who is established at the right hand of the Power, or with which he will come, or to which the truth of God will reach, according to what is written: "and your truth reaches even to the clouds"? These are the living clouds, the prophets of God and the apostles of Christ, whom he commands to rain when it is fitting, or not to rain upon the vineyard without fruit. But if anyone does not wish to be a cloud of this kind, upon which and with which the Son of Man will come when he appears, let him himself take heed. For he always comes upon those and with those, showing his coming to those worthy of him — God the Word and Wisdom and Truth and Righteousness. And these clouds which we have handed down, as though bearing "the image of the heavenly", are clouds of the heaven that does not pass away, made worthy of the seat of God and the kingdom of God, as "heirs of God and coheirs of Christ", and they reign together with him.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Then the chief priest tore his garments, saying: he has blasphemed (26, 65ᵃ).

While the Lord was prophesying these things, that priest, the Lord's enemy — as one who was not near enough to see the Son of Man and the Power at whose right hand he was seated, as one bent down and unable to look upward, not hearing the things he was saying — tore his garments, displaying his own foulness and the nakedness of his soul, and making manifest a mystery: that the old priesthood was to be torn asunder, along with the robe of his priesthood and of the worship which had been according to the letter.

But he judged the greatness of Christ's words to be blasphemy, and he esteemed as glory the Jewish and fabulous history of the letter that kills. And he supposed (as though he understood) that Christ's discourses were sufficient as testimony against him — those very discourses which were witnesses of his divinity (as far as concerns those who are able to understand). And he says to those who were of the same mind: behold, now you have heard his blasphemy; what does it seem to you. Until, answering, they too pronounce against their own soul concerning Jesus, that he is guilty of death. How great, do you think, was the error, to pronounce Life itself, the principal Life of all, guilty of death, and by the testimony of so many rising again not to behold the fountain of life, from which life flowed forth into all the living, seeing that "as the Father has life in himself, so also he has granted to the Son to have life in himself"?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: How great their error! to pronounce the principle of all men's life to be guilty of death, and not to acknowledge by the testimony of the resurrection of so many, the Fount of life, from Whom life flows to all that rise again.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Then they spat in his face and struck him with their fists. But others slapped his face with the palms of their hands, saying: Prophesy to us, O Christ, who is it that struck you? (26, 67. 68)

Most wickedly, as I judge, did those who had heard Jesus saying: "yet I say to you, that from now on you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven" dare to spit in his face. For they supposed that by this they would confound him as a liar, and that one who sat "at the right hand of power" and was to come "in the clouds" would not endure the reproach of being spat upon; for they were ignorant of the words of the prophet Isaiah, who prophesied these very same things concerning him, and said in the person of the Lord and Savior himself: "what, that I came, and there was no man? I called, and there was none who would obey? Is my hand not able to rescue? Or can I not deliver? Behold, at my rebuke I will make the sea a desert, and I will set the rivers a desert. And their fish shall be dried up because they have no water, and shall die of thirst. And I will clothe the heaven with darkness, and make its covering like sackcloth. The Lord gives me the tongue of instruction, that I may know how it behooves me to speak the word; he set me in the morning, he applied to me an ear to hear, and the instruction of the Lord shall open my ears; but I am not unbelieving, nor do I contradict. I offered my back to the scourges, and my cheeks to the palms of hands, but I did not turn away my face from the confusion of spittings, and the Lord God became my helper". For all who are of the Church confess him to be Christ who says: "the Lord, the Lord gave me the tongue of instruction" and the rest which I have expounded.

But I have fittingly expounded also those things which above were joined to these, wishing to show that this was prophesied concerning that glorious one, that he should be spat upon and buffeted. For to what other does it fit to say: "I came", except to Christ who came into the world? Or whom did it befit to say: "I called, and there was none who would obey", except him who came to call the people of the Jews and was not heard, and therefore did not rescue the people nor deliver it, but forsook it? And it is Christ who says: "behold, at my rebuke I will make the sea a desert, and I will set the rivers a desert", who is to bring about the consummation of the world. For it is he who will clothe the heaven with "darkness" and clothe it "as with sackcloth", and, receiving from the Father the "tongue of instruction", knew how "it behooved him to speak the word" which God had entrusted to him; and "he applied to him an ear", that he might hear more than all who hear, and the "instruction" of the Father opened his ear, because he was not unbelieving to the Father who sent him nor contradicting, and by the very deed he taught those desiring to learn meekness and praiseworthy humility. And there was a work in this, that he taught these things by deeds, offering his "back to the scourges and his cheeks to the palms of hands" and not turning away his face "from the confusion of spittings", so that us (as I judge), who had all been worthy to suffer these disgraces, he himself might rescue by suffering them for us. For he did "not die for us", that we might not die, but that we might not die for ourselves; and he was struck with blows for us and was spat upon, so that we, who had been worthy of all these things on account of our sins, might not suffer them, but that, suffering them for righteousness, we might receive them gladly. And Paul indeed says of the Savior, that "he humbled himself, being made obedient unto death, even the death of the cross". For it is not unseemly for one who wishes to number in how many things Christ humbled himself, to count out (beyond those things which Paul expounded, saying: "he humbled himself, being made obedient unto death"): unto the "palms of hands", unto the "confusion of spittings" and of "scourges" and of death, on account of all which "God exalted him". For it was not on account of death alone which he bore for us that he exalted him, but also on account of the palms and the spittings and the rest.

But that the injury of spittings is taken as the extreme injury, is manifest also in the law, in which it is written that the wife of a deceased man, if the brother of her husband will not take her, going to him who refused to take her to himself as wife, in the presence of the elders shall unshoe "one of his sandals from his feet and shall spit in his face and shall say: so shall it be done to the man who has not built up the house of his brother". Therefore Christ did not turn away his face "from the confusion of spittings", that his countenance might be more glorified than the countenance of Moses was glorified, with so great and such glory that (by comparison with this glorification) the glorification of that countenance is done away, just as in the sight of the sun the light of a lamp is done away, and just as the knowledge which is in part is done away "when that which is perfect has come". But they also struck with their fists the holy head of the Church, on account of which they themselves are buffeted by Satan, not that they may not be exalted nor that their strength may be made perfect, but that, handed over to the enemy and avenger, they may receive back the sin which they committed in buffeting Jesus. And not content only to spit in his face and to strike him with their fists, they still further struck him with the palms of their hands and, mocking him, said: prophesy to us, who struck you. On account of which they received an eternal blow, and were deprived of all prophecy, struck and chastised, and even so not willing to receive instruction, according to what Jeremiah had prophesied of this very thing concerning them: "you scourged them and they did not grieve, and they refused to receive instruction". And now those who do injury to some one person of the Church and do these things to him, spit in the face of Christ and, striking Christ with their fists, chastise him also with the palms of their hands.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Or, By the first handmaid is understood the Synagogue of the Jews, which oft compelled the faithful to deny; by the second, the congregations of the Gentiles, who even persecuted the Christians; they that stood in the hall signify the ministers of divers heresies, who also compel men to deny the truth of Christ.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
But Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard; and one of the maidservants came to him, saying: You too were with Jesus the Galilean. But he denied it before them all, saying: I do not know what you are saying. And as he was going out to the gate, another maidservant saw him and said to him there: This man too was with Jesus the Nazarene. And again he denied it with an oath, saying, I do not know the man. And after a little while those who were standing there came and said to Peter: Truly you are one of them, for even your speech makes you plain. Then he began to curse and to swear, saying, I do not know the man. And immediately a cock crowed. And Peter remembered the word of Jesus who had said to him: Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times; and going out he wept most bitterly.

Considering Peter's denial more fully, we say that "no one can call Jesus Lord except in the Holy Spirit" (as Paul teaches us), and "the Holy Spirit was not yet then" in men "because Jesus had not yet been glorified" (as John says), and therefore it was not possible that even such a Peter should then confess Jesus. Nor yet was he to be blamed for not confessing Jesus, since to those who confess it is said: "It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you".

But we, since that Spirit of our Father is able to speak in us, and since it is in our power to give "place" in us to the Holy Spirit and not to "the devil", if we deny him, we shall have no excuse.

Perhaps, moreover, whoever is in the courtyard of Caiaphas "the chief priest" cannot confess the Lord Jesus unless he has gone out of his courtyard and been made to be outside of every doctrine that is contrary to Jesus and that hands down Jewish traditions—and this not according to the will of the Scriptures, but according to "the commandments and teachings of men". For consider that Peter, sitting outside, separated from Jesus and set in the courtyard of the chief priest, denied Jesus before them all; and again a second time, likewise, being not yet made to be outside beyond the gate, but wishing to go out and not yet having gone out, denied him at the gate; but also a third time, when those who were standing said: Truly you are one of them, and when he began to curse himself and to swear, saying, I do not know the man, he was still not outside. And all these denials were made by him in the night and in darkness, before day comes and the sign of day, that is, the cock's crow which rouses from sleep those who are willing. And, to speak by way of example, if Peter had denied him after the cock's crow—so that it might be said: "the night has advanced, and the day has drawn near, let us walk becomingly as in the day"—Peter would have been worthy of no excuse.

But perhaps also all men, when they deny Jesus in such a way that the sin of their denial may receive healing, are seen to deny him before the cock's crow, when the sun of righteousness has not yet risen upon them nor its rising drawn near to them. But if, after the rising of such a sun upon the soul, "we sin willingly after we have received the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains for us a sacrifice for sin, but a fearful judgment and a zeal of fire, which is to consume the enemies".

And indeed in the case of Peter, then denying, it was not fitting to say: "how do you not think that they deserve worse punishments who have trodden underfoot the Son of God and have esteemed the blood of the covenant common, by which they were sanctified, and have done injury to the Spirit of grace?"; for Peter had not yet been sanctified by the blood of Christ (which was the blood of the new covenant), nor did he do injury to the Spirit of grace which from the beginning he had not even received, since "Jesus had not yet been glorified", "nor was" the "Holy Spirit" in men.

But if in us this impious sin of denial has been committed, it is fitting to say all these things, since we have both been sanctified by the blood of the covenant and have received the "Spirit of grace". Therefore to esteem the most precious "blood of the covenant" as "common" and to do injury to the Spirit of grace is worse than all sins, so that we can receive remission "neither in this age nor in the age to come", if we deny the Son of God. Since therefore for us "the night has advanced, and the day has drawn near" and the sign of day, the cock's crow, has sounded to us, therefore let us stand "even unto blood, contending against sin", and for the sake of the charity that never falls away let us endure all things, that with those perfected in it we may obtain the inheritance. And mark this, that before the cock's crow, and before the Holy Spirit, and in the time of deep night, even if someone should deny frequently, he can live; which is plain from the fact that Peter denied three times. But if after the cock's crow someone, even once, being set in whatever peril, should deny, "it is impossible for him to be renewed unto repentance, so as to crucify again to himself the Son of God". But whoever has been caught in such a sin of denial, let him look upon that which is written: "woe to those who draw their sins to themselves as with a long rope, and their iniquities as with the strap of a yoke of a calf", and let him not say: "our sins are upon us, and how shall we live? As I live, says the Lord, since I do not will the death of the sinner, but rather his repentance". But God himself knows—of whom it is written: "and he, being wise, will bring evils upon them"—what kind of evils he will bring upon those who deny and do not repent, and what kind upon those who deny and do repent, and what kind of good things upon those who have never denied him either in word "before men" or in works. And let us become far removed from the first maidservant and from the other, and from all who stand in his courtyard or at his gate, that we may not be near to those who cause the one who is beside them to deny him. But we shall know who the maidservant of the chief priest is, if we understand who the maidservant of God is, of whom it is written: "I am your servant and the son of your maidservant".

And you will be able to know what the courtyards of the chief priest are, if you understand what the courtyards of the house of God are, of which it is written: "behold now, bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord", "you who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courtyards of the house of our God". But if we must also say something about the other maidservant, so that we may withdraw from her as well, let us understand what is written: "as the eyes of a maidservant are upon the hands of her mistress, so are our eyes toward the Lord our God, until he have mercy upon us". I think the first maidservant of the chief priest, who causes the disciples of Christ to deny him, is to be understood as the synagogue of the Jews "according to the flesh", who have frequently compelled the faithful to deny; and the second maidservant as the assembly of the Gentiles, who, themselves also persecuting Christians, compelled them to deny; and the third, those standing in the courtyards, are the ministers of the various heresies, who themselves also compel men to deny the truth of Christ. But in the night Peter not only denies three times, but even curses himself and swears that I do not know the man. And indeed then he still knew Christ "according to the flesh", nor could he yet say: "even if we have known Christ at some time according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him thus"; for as long as the sign of day did not yet exist, Peter in denying was not mindful of the words of Jesus, but after the angel of day cried out to him, then he remembered the word of Jesus who said to him: before the cock crows, you will deny me three times. And when he remembered the word of Christ, he was no longer in the courtyard of the chief priest nor beside his gate, but outside; otherwise he would by no means have wept, for thus it is written: going out he wept most bitterly. Therefore, as according to Luke the "sinful woman" beside the feet of the Lord "wept" in repentance, so here Peter, having gone out of the courtyard of the chief priest to his gate, weeps from the bitterness of sin, making his weeping bitter in repentance.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
But when morning had come, all the chief priests and elders of the people took counsel against Jesus, that they might deliver him to death; and they led him away bound and delivered him to Pontius Pilate the governor (27, 1. 2).

He who stumbles in the darkness and at night is worthy of pardon, but he who stumbles in the clear daylight can never blame his error as though it belonged to one who is master of himself (especially when he stumbles while having within himself the "lamp of the body"), but rather he must blame his own lack of self-mastery. Now we have said this to show that the disciples of Christ are indeed scandalized in the night, according to what the Lord foretells to them: "you will all suffer scandal because of me on this night", and because Peter denied three times before the cock crowed. But those who take counsel against Jesus — all the chief priests and elders of the people, when morning had come — sin in the light, that is, knowingly, according to what is written concerning this counsel, that they took counsel with one accord "together", as it is written in the Psalms, that they might deliver Christ to death, thinking to extinguish through his death his teaching and the faith in him among those who had believed in him as in the Son of God.

But taking such counsel against him, the chief priests of the cult of the letter that kills, and the elders of the ministry of condemnation, bound Jesus, who looses men from their bonds and "says to those who are in bonds: come forth", and who looses those who are fettered and says: "let us break their bonds asunder, and let us cast their yoke from us", and who had loosed from her bonds "the daughter of Abraham" bound by Satan "for eighteen years", so that she who "before could not at all look upward" should now be no longer bent down. And they bound him who willed it, and who, in the very fact that he was bound, was laying an ambush against those very bonds and breaking them, so that now the chief priests and elders of the Jews should have no bonds against men, the Lord evidently breaking them in himself.

But if anyone requires of me a Scripture showing these things concerning the breaking of the bonds with which the chief priests and elders bound Jesus, let him understand that for this very reason Jesus himself says through the prophet: "let us break their bonds asunder", as if he were speaking of the chief priests and elders, or much more of those rulers who wrought in them, and of the kings of the earth, those who "stood up", and of the princes who "came together as one against the Lord and against his Christ", whose "yoke also let us cast from us". But he will satisfy you still further, so that you may accept that, even though those who took counsel against him led Jesus away bound, nevertheless Jesus broke the bonds, if you consider the things that are written concerning Samson, who was frequently bound and broke the bonds of the foreigners, because he had been a Nazarite of God and had hair full of strength. If therefore that man, on account of the strength of the hair which he had on his head, was able to break the bonds of the foreigners with which they had frequently bound him, how much more Christ, who after so many wonders and mighty works which he did, willingly delivered himself over to bonds (lulling to sleep within himself the power of his divinity and consenting to be bound), without doubt broke the bonds surrounding him! Of which bonds the bonds of Samson were the mysteries.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: and they handed him over to Pontius Pilate. But whether both names of the governor also have some meaning fitting the dispensation of the Lord and Savior, or not, is not easy to answer with any finality. For the root terms from which these names are derived may move someone — Pontius and Pilatus; but whether one is rightly moved or not, let each of those capable of it come to consider and know.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: They supposed that by His death they should crush His doctrine, and the belief in Him of those who believed Him to be the Son of God. With such purpose against Him they bound Jesus, Who looses them that are bound. (vid. Isa. 61:1.)

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let the propounders of those fables concerning intrinsically evil naturesa answer me here, whence Judas came to the acknowledgment of his sin, I have sinned in that I have betrayed righteous blood, except through the good mind originally implanted in him, and that seed of virtue which is sown in every rational soul? But Judas did not cherish this, and so fell into this sin. But if ever any man was made of a nature that was to perish, Judas was yet more of such a nature. If indeed he had done this after Christ's resurrection, it might have been said, that the power of the resurrection brought him to repentance. But he repented when he saw Christ delivered up to Pilate, perhaps remembering the things Jesus had so often spoken of His resurrection. (John 13:27.) Or, perhaps Satan who had entered into him continued with him till Jesus was given up to Pilate, and then, having accomplished his purpose, departed from him; whereupon he repented. But how could Judas know that He was condemned, for He had not yet been examined by Pilate? One may perhaps say, that he foreboded the event in his own mind from the very first, when he saw Him delivered up. Another may explain the words, when he saw that he was condemned, of Judas himself, that he then perceived his evil case, and saw that he himself was condemned.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Then Judas, who betrayed him, seeing that he was condemned, led by repentance brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and the elders, saying: I have sinned in that I betrayed innocent blood. But they said: What is that to us? See thou to it. And casting down the pieces of silver in the temple, he departed, and going away hanged himself with a noose. But the chief priests, having taken the pieces of silver, said: It is not lawful to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood. And having taken counsel together, they bought with them the potter's field, for the burial of strangers. For this reason that field was called Acheldemach, that is, the field of blood, unto this present day. Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremiah the prophet, saying: And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him that was priced, whom they priced of the sons of Israel, and gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord appointed me.

Let those answer me who introduce certain fables concerning natures, supposing that they speak the truth and not recognizing that their opinion accuses the Creator of injustice, as one who made certain vessels indeed "unto honor" not by reason of any virtue of theirs leading them to honor, but certain others "unto dishonor" not because of their sins leading them to dishonor. For if Judas was of a perishable nature, how did he take up so great a repentance that he was not overcome by desire of the thirty pieces of silver, for the sake of which he took up the impious audacity of the betrayal? For if they refer to the property of natures what is said: "a bad tree cannot bring forth good fruits", let them say — unless he breathe forth some goodness, even if not perfectly nor as he ought, Judas being converted: this very thing, that he brought back the thirty pieces of silver, whence is it, and that he said, recognizing his sin: I have sinned in betraying innocent blood, unless it be from a good planting of the mind and from the sowing of virtue, which is sown in every rational soul, which Judas did not cultivate and therefore fell into such a sin? But if any of men is of a perishing nature, without doubt Judas too was rather of a nature of this perishing kind. And this without doubt would seem to have been the case, if, betraying innocent blood, he had either not brought back the money, taking his delight in it, or, bringing it back, had not said that I have sinned in betraying innocent blood.

And if indeed Judas had said what he said after the resurrection of Christ from the dead, perhaps it would plausibly have to be said that the very power of his resurrection compelled him to repent of the deed and to confess his sin. But as it is, as soon as he saw that he had been delivered up to Pilate, being stung with compunction he repented; and perhaps also remembering those things which Jesus had frequently said to his disciples concerning his future resurrection. Judas therefore, seeing the greatness of his crime, did indeed repent and spoke out of the repentance of his heart, confessing his sin, in that he had betrayed innocent blood, "but he did not repent also according to knowledge", as he ought to have repented. For he supposed that he would anticipate in death his master who was about to die, and would meet him with a naked soul, so that, confessing and imploring, he might obtain mercy. For which reason he himself judged and condemned himself in that he had sinned knowingly, and he did not look to what Job had said, when set in such great disasters: "would that I might be able to kill myself, or to ask someone to do this for me", nor did he see that it does not befit a servant of God to expel himself from this life, but rather to await concerning this too the judgment of God.

Let us now see whether (that which lies hidden from many … of that passage) by God's granting we may be able to explain what is said: But Judas, who betrayed him, seeing that he was condemned, led by repentance brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests, and the rest. For if it had been written, after the sentence of Pilate, after he delivered Jesus, scourged with whips, to the Jews that they might crucify him, that Judas had done these things, we should without doubt seek nothing of this kind in that which is said: seeing that he was condemned. But as it is, how did Judas see that he was condemned (for Jesus had not yet been condemned nor questioned by Pilate)? Perhaps therefore someone will say (doing violence to the text) that by the consideration of his own mind he saw the "outcome" of the matter, that he was condemned, from this, that he beheld him delivered up by the chief priests and the elders of the people. But another will say in this way, that what is written: But Judas, seeing that he was condemned, refers to Judas himself. For when the chief priests and the elders of the people had delivered Jesus to Pilate, then Judas felt his own evil and understood that one who had dared such things was without doubt judged and condemned by God. And perhaps Satan too, who after the dipped bread had entered into Judas, was present with him until Jesus should be delivered to Pilate. But after he had done what he wished, "he departed from him"; and, the devil departing, he understood and saw that, betraying innocent blood, he was condemned by God, and his understanding, being now at leisure and no longer having the devil working within him, was able to understand. He was able therefore, the devil departing from him, to receive repentance and to bring back the thirty pieces of silver to those who had given them. And he was able to say, the devil departing, what before the devil departed from him he could not have said; for while the devil was still filling his heart he could not say: I have sinned in betraying innocent blood. But we do not say this, that the devil, departing from any such man, thereafter by no means lies in wait for him. Rather he watches again for the time, whether he may again be able to set himself upon him; and after someone has come to recognize [the devil] even in accordance with his own sin, the devil watches also for the place of a third deception in him.

But if it is needful to use examples as well, let us consider in the first epistle to the Corinthians him who "had his father's wife", for in such an evil he could not have been without a great working of the devil. Of which evil he repented, as the Scripture itself testifies, and was made sorrowful with a "sorrow according to God", a sorrow "which works repentance unto stable salvation". But after he took up such sorrow, the devil set himself upon him again, wishing to exaggerate that sorrow of his beyond measure, so that the sorrow itself should no longer be "according to God", but that, being made more abundant, it might swallow up the sorrowing man beyond measure and beyond what he ought to have sorrowed, and thus Satan might swallow him up in "more abundant sorrow". Foreknowing which, the Apostle gives counsel to the Corinthians that they should confirm "love toward him", stating this as the cause: "lest", he says, "he who is such be swallowed up by more abundant sorrow"; "for we are not ignorant of his devices". Something similar happened also in the case of Judas, who betrayed Jesus, and according to the likeness of that sorrow "which works repentance unto stable salvation", he too being made sorrowful, after he was led by repentance, brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests, saying: I have sinned in betraying innocent blood. Which very thing belonged to repentance and to saving sorrow; but because he never kept his heart, nor sorrowed wisely, but took up a more abundant sorrow sent under to him by the devil (who wished to swallow him up in "more abundant sorrow"), therefore, bringing back those pieces of silver into the temple, he went away and hanged himself with a noose. For if, after he brought back the money and confessed that he had sinned in that he betrayed innocent blood, he had not gone away and hanged himself with a noose, but had sought a "place of repentance" and awaited the time of repentance, perhaps he would even have found him who said: "as I live, since I do not will the death of the sinner, but rather his repentance".

But I think that Judas, understanding also something greater concerning the Savior, cast the thirty pieces of silver nowhere else but into the temple, where he knew the Lord had by his act cast out of the temple "the sheep and the oxen", and had said "to the sellers of doves: take these things hence, and make not my Father's house a house of merchandise". Despairing enough of himself, therefore, because he understood the greatness of his sin, casting those pieces of silver into the temple, he departed and hanged himself with a noose. But those who took up those pieces of silver wished to observe something lawful, and not to put them into the treasury, where the gifts of the people for the needs of the poor were gathered; for they deemed it impious to put the price of blood into the treasury. For which reason, taking counsel, they purchased with that money the potter's field, of one who works clay; for they saw that it was more fitting for that money to be spent upon the dead and upon the place of the dead and of burial, since it was the price of blood, than in the treasury or in some honorable need. But because among the places of the dead too there are differences (since many indeed according to their wish are desirably buried in their own ancestral monuments, while some, on account of certain calamities, are frequently buried in foreign monuments), therefore those who took up the price of the blood of Jesus used it for the purchase of the field of some potter, that in it foreign dead might be buried, not according to their wish but earning this according to some adverse chance. But if it is fitting to understand the strangers spiritually also, we say that the strangers are those who unto the end are estranged from God and are strangers to his covenants. Such strangers therefore have an end of this kind, that they should be buried in the potter's field, which was purchased with the price of blood. For the righteous are they who say: "we have been buried together" with Christ "in the new monument which is found hewn in the rock", "in the hewn monument, where none yet of the dead has been laid". But those who unto the end are strangers from Christ and aliens from God will say, without doubt, consequently: "we have been buried together" with the strangers in the field of the potter who works clay, which was purchased with the price of blood, and we are in the field which is named the field of blood.

But since what the evangelist says after these things (then was fulfilled that which had been spoken by Jeremiah the prophet, saying the things which are written) — this is not found to have been prophesied by Jeremiah anywhere in his books, whether those which are read in the churches or those which are recited among the Jews — but if anyone can know, let him show where it is written. I suspect, however, that either it is an error of the Scripture and Jeremiah is put for Zechariah, or that there is some secret writing of Jeremiah in which it is written. Now such is the text in Zechariah the prophet: "and I will say to them: if it is good in your sight, give me my wages, or refuse them; and they appointed my wages, thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me: put them down into the furnace, and see if it is genuine, even as I was proved for their sake. And I took the thirty pieces of silver, and put them into the house of the Lord, into the furnace". But if anyone saying this supposes that he stumbles, let him see whether this may be prophesied somewhere in the secret writings of Jeremiah, knowing that the Apostle too brings forward certain writings of the secret books, as he says somewhere: "what eye has not seen nor ear heard"; for in no canonical book is this found set down, except in the secret writings of Elijah the prophet. Likewise what he says: "as Jamnes and Mambres withstood Moses" is not found in the public books, but in the secret book which is entitled the book of Jamnes and Mambres. Whence some have dared to reject the epistle to Timothy as having in itself the text of some secret writing, but they were not able to; but that anyone rejected the first epistle to the Corinthians on this account as spurious, has never come to my ears.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But when the Devil leaves any one, he watches his time for return, and having taken it, he leads him into a second sin, and then watches for opportunity for a third deceit. (1 Cor. 5:1.) So the man who had married his father's wife afterwards repented him of this sin, but again the Devil resolved so to augment this very sorrow of repentance, that his sorrow being made too abundant might swallow up the sorrower. Something like this took place in Judas, who after his repentance did not preserve his own heart, but received that more abundant sorrow supplied to him by the Devil, who sought to swallow him up, as it follows, And he went out, and hanged himself. But had he desired and looked for place and time for repentance, he would perhaps have found Him who has said, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked. (Ezek. 33:11.) Or, perhaps, he desired to die before his Master on His way to death, and to meet Him with a disembodied spirit, that by confession and deprecation he might obtain mercy; and did not see that it is not fitting that a servant of God should dismiss himself from life, but should wait God's sentence.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
They thought it meet to spend upon the dead that money which was the price of blood. But as there are differences even in burial places, they used the price of Jesus' blood in the purchase of some potter's field, where foreigners might be buried, not as they desired in the sepulchres of their fathers.

Or, the foreigners are they who to the end are aliens from God, for the righteous are buried with Christ in a new tomb hewn out in the rock. But they who are aliens from God, even to the end, are buried in the field of a potter, a worker in clay, which being bought by the price of blood, is called the field of blood.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
They thought it meet to spend upon the dead that money which was the price of blood. But as there are differences even in burial places, they used the price of Jesus' blood in the purchase of some potter's field, where foreigners might be buried, not as they desired in the sepulchres of their fathers.

Or, the foreigners are they who to the end are aliens from God, for the righteous are buried with Christ in a new tomb hewn out in the rock. But they who are aliens from God, even to the end, are buried in the field of a potter, a worker in clay, which being bought by the price of blood, is called the field of blood.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Mark how He that is ordained by His Father to be the Judge of the whole creation, humbled Himself, and was content to stand before the judge of the land of Judæa, and to be asked by Pilate either in mockery or doubt, Art thou the King of the Jews?

Or, Pilate spoke this affirmatively, as he afterwards wrote in the inscription, The King of the Jews. By answering to the Chief Priest, Thou hast said, He indirectly reproved his doubts, but now He turns Pilate's speech into an affirmative, Jesus saith unto him, Thou sayest it.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
But Jesus stood before the governor; and the governor questioned him, saying: Are you the king of the Jews? Jesus says to him: You say so. Truly Jesus "did not count it robbery that he was equal to God", and not once but frequently he humbled himself for the sake of men. And now therefore, having been "appointed judge of all creation" by the Father, the King of kings and Lord of lords, see to how great a degree he humbled himself, so that he consented to stand before the judge of the land of Judea at that time, and being summoned he was questioned with a question which Pilate perhaps in derision or in doubt asked, saying: Are you the king of the Jews? To which question he answered what he thought fitting, saying You say so. And when he was put on oath by the high priest, that he should say whether he himself is the Christ the Son of God, he answered: "You have said it", but when questioned by Pilate Are you the king of the Jews? he answered You say so. Consider the questions: was not that question, "whether you are the Christ the Son of God", suited to a Jewish person, whereas to the Roman judge saying interrogatively no longer: You are the Christ, but: Are you the king of the Jews?

But whoever carefully considers the very fine points of the Gospel words will see that the high priest indeed said doubtingly: "if you are the Christ the Son of God" (for the syllable "if" shows the doubt of the questioning), but Pilate said declaratively: You are the king of the Jews. And that Pilate said this declaratively, this too is confirmed by the fact that he also elsewhere inscribes above, in the title, "King of the Jews" in three languages, "in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin", so that both Hebrews and Greeks and Romans might know that Pilate too knew him to be the king of the Jews. For which reason it appears with what reverence he inquired concerning Jesus and appealed to the people, that they should ask rather for Jesus to be released than Barabbas. And it was also a sign of Pilate's reverence, that washing his hands he said: "I am innocent of the blood of this man; see you to it".

But that he said to the high priest "you have said it", obliquely reproving his doubt, he refutes it, and that he says to Pilate you say so, he confirms the opinion of the one making a declaration. But Mark, instead of "if you are the Christ the Son of God", writes thus: "are you the Son of the Blessed?" Perhaps either that which is written simply, or this which is written doubtingly — I do not know whether the copies may not have an error, since both ought equally to have said: "if you are", or both: "you are".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Neither then nor now did Jesus make any reply to their accusations, for the word of God was not sent to them, as it was formerly to the Prophets. Neither was Pilate worthy of an answer, as he had no fixed or abiding opinion of Christ, but veered about to contradictory suppositions. Hearest thou not how many things they witness against thee?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
And when he was accused by the chief priests and elders of the people, he answered nothing. Then Pilate says to him: Do you not hear how many testimonies they bring against you? And he did not answer him a single word, so that the governor marveled exceedingly.

The ministers of the Jewish letter that kills, and the elders, are the sons of those priests and elders who accused Jesus, taking up their accusation even until now and accusing Jesus. Therefore, since that very sin remains in them, and "wrath, even to the end" has once forestalled them, they still suffer those same workings, being abandoned along with the whole people "like a tent in a vineyard, and like a hut in a cucumber-field, and like a city that is stormed." And just as Jesus, when accused, then answered nothing, so also now against the accusations of those priests and elders he answers nothing. For the Word of God is silent toward them, and they no longer hear the Word of God, as had once come to pass with the prophets, and, in the consummation of the ages, when he "was made flesh and dwelt among us."

And not only to the chief priests and elders of the people falsely accusing him did he not respond,

but neither to Pilate, since he wished to hear him defending himself against their lying accusations. For when Pilate said to him, after the accusations of the chief priests and elders: Do you not hear how many things they accuse you of?—

not even to him did he respond. For it was not fitting to respond even to one who was in doubt as to whether he ought to respond against their false accusations.

This we have said not forgetting what was said about Pilate, namely that he had at least some momentary kindly disposition toward Christ (for that this is true of Pilate is shown from the whole narrative concerning him).

Yet no one will dare to say that the judgment about Christ within him was abiding and firm; for he was being drawn also to the contrary. Therefore now too, to one being drawn toward the worse opinion, the Lord did not respond, despising all the things that had been said in accusation of him.

But Pilate marveled at his constancy, perhaps knowing how, though he was competent to pronounce sentence and to remit the charge … he marveled, seeing him stand in the calm and quiet gravity of wisdom and, with judgment, unperturbed—he in whom it was reckoned by those who were there that he was in peril of death; and he was stronger than human nature,

and, though all its weakness sought to blunt the power of his spirit, it did not prevail to do this.

But the fact that it is written that Pilate did not only marvel, but even marveled exceedingly, moves me to reckon that it seemed to him worthy of great wonder that Christ, when brought forward to a criminal trial, should remain unperturbed and stand before death, which among all men is reckoned terrible.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The governor marvelled at His endurance, as knowing that he had power to condemn Him, He yet continued in a peaceful, placid, and immovable prudence and gravity. He marvelled greatly, for it seemed to him a great miracle that Christ, produced before a criminal tribunal, stood thus fearless of death, which all men think so terrible.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Now at the feast day the governor was accustomed to release to the people one prisoner, whomever they wished.

Do not be surprised if, the Roman rule still being in its beginnings among them, and the Jews newly taking up the yoke of the Romans, since it had been granted to the Jews that at the paschal solemnity they might ask for one whom they wished,

even though he seemed liable for a thousand murders. For thus the nations render certain favors to those whom they subject to themselves, until their yoke is confirmed over them. Yet this custom of releasing a prisoner existed at one time also among the Jews. For when Saul had decreed that no one should take food, but Jonathan had tasted a honeycomb against the king's decree, he found Jonathan liable; and although he was his appointed son, yet on account of some oath of his he had decreed to put him to death. But he did not kill him, since all the people of Israel intervened and asked for him to be granted his life.

But that Pilate released one prisoner to the people, or that Saul, at the people's request, released Jonathan, is no wonder; for the life of both those who were asking was under fault, since the Jews were always liable. But let us inquire whether something of this sort happens also in the judgment of God, so that the whole Church may be able to ask that some sinner be freed from the condemnation of sin — and especially if perhaps he has all the remaining works of perdition, yet is unwearied in doing good to the Church. For you will find such men often set in positions of power: sinners indeed in other respects, yet doing much on behalf of Christians as far as it is possible for them. And you will be led the more to inquire into such matters, if it has a fitting rationale, seeing that Israel too used to pray to God "for the life of Nebuchadnezzar" and of Belshazzar his son. But this, if it seems to anyone worthy of inquiry, let him inquire into it. But as for what is plain, let us all try to take care that we be found to be among those who ask, and in the rank of those who have lived well, rather than among those on whose behalf petition is made as for evil men. For even if one of the sinners is granted to the prayers of the Church, it is nevertheless not just that such a one should attain glory and blessedness; for it is enough that he be released from punishment.

But I think, on account of that festival of the Jews on which Barabbas was chosen for life while Christ was neglected, the Lord says through the prophet: "my soul hates your fasts and your holidays and your feast days". And because they preferred to keep the solemnity with the robber set free rather than with Jesus, I will speak by way of example: if they had kept the solemnity rightly, like Josiah or someone similar to him, and there had been given to them the liberty of asking for whomever they wished, without doubt they would have demanded Jesus and condemned Barabbas. But let us pray that, as we keep the festal day, "not in the old leaven nor in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth", we may deserve indeed to condemn Barabbas, but to receive Jesus, free from all bonds, as our king and lord. And as long as we do these things, our festal days will not be turned into mourning, nor our songs into lamentation, but there will be in us true solemnities, the solemnities of God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Thus do the Gentiles show favours to those whom they subject to themselves, until their yoke is riveted. Yet did this practice obtain also among the Jews, Saul did not put Jonathan to death, because all the people sought his life. (1 Sam. 14.)

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Now at that time they had a notorious prisoner, who was called Barabbas. So when they were gathered together, Pilate said to them: Whom do you wish that I release to you, Jesus Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ? For he knew that they had handed him over out of envy.

In many copies it is not contained that Barabbas was also called Jesus, and perhaps rightly so, that the name of Jesus might not belong to any of the wicked. For in so great a multitude of the Scriptures we know of no Jesus who was a sinner, whereas in other names we find that, among the righteous, there are also found wicked men of the very same name — for instance, Judas the apostle, the zealot, and likewise Judas the patriarch, and Judas Maccabaeus, all praiseworthy, but also Judas the traitor; and in Genesis there are found sons of Seth and sons of Cain bearing the same name, such as Enoch and Lamech and Methuselah. But it was not fitting that there should be any such thing also in the name of Jesus. And I think that in the heresies some such thing has been added on, so that they might have something apt to say for their fables about the likeness of the name of Jesus and Barabbas. For I judge that in these matters some mystery is set forth: that Barabbas was appointed for sedition and wars and murders to be committed in the souls of men, but Jesus, as the Son of God and peace, was appointed, and as the Word and Wisdom, for all good things. These two, then, being bound in human affairs and bodies, that people demanded for itself that Barabbas be released; on whose account that nation does not cease to have seditions and murders and robberies — according to some of that nation in the things that are held outwardly, but according to all the Jews who do not believe in Jesus, inwardly in the soul. For where Jesus is not, there are seditions and quarrels and battles; but where Jesus is, so that they can say: "but if Christ is in us, the body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness", there all good things are together, and innumerable spiritual riches are in his hands, and peace; "for he himself is our peace, who has made both one". And if anyone should behold that contrary operation, he will recognize that it is he who is in men the bound notorious Barabbas, whom they desire to be released for themselves — not only Israel then sinning according to the flesh, but also all who are like him either in doctrine or in life. Whoever, therefore, does evil things, in his body Barabbas is released, but Christ is bound; but whoever does good things, to him Christ is released, but Barabbas is bound.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Thus it is plainly seen how the Jewish people is moved by its elders and the doctors of the Jewish system, and stirred up against Jesus to destroy Him.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Now while he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent to him, saying: Have nothing to do with that just man; for I have suffered many things this day in a dream because of him.

And Jesus indeed had been handed over out of envy, and out of such manifest envy that even Pilate was not unaware of it. But the evangelist wished not to pass over a matter of divine providence that contains praise of God, who willed through a dream to convert Pilate's wife, so that, as far as lay in her, she might forbid her husband to dare to pronounce sentence against Jesus. And Matthew did not indeed set forth the dream, but only said that she had suffered many things in a dream because of Jesus, and therefore she suffered in a dream so that she might not suffer further. So that we may call Pilate's wife blessed, who suffered many things in a dream because of Jesus, and received in a dream what she was going to suffer.

From which someone will dare to say that it is better for a person to receive evils in a dream than to receive them in real life. For who would not choose to receive his evils in a dream rather than to receive them in his life (unless perhaps he deserves such things that it is expedient for him to receive harsher things in his life rather than to receive lighter ones in a dream)? For he who has received evils in his life (and not these evils which he received in his dream) is consoled and rests "in the bosom of Abraham", according to which he will also have consolation. But whether she also had the beginning of her conversion to God from the fact that she had suffered many things because of Jesus in a dream, God knows; yet this too is contained in certain writings that are not public.

And see (because Pilate's wife called Jesus just) whether perhaps this wife of Pilate is a mystery of the Church from the Gentiles, which at one time indeed was ruled by Pilate, but now is no longer under him because of her faith in Christ.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
But the chief priests and the elders persuaded the people to ask for Barabbas, but to destroy Jesus. And the governor answering said to them: Which of the two do you wish that I release to you? But they said: Barabbas.

And it is possible to see even now how the people of the Jews are persuaded and stirred up by their elders and by the teachers of the Jewish worship against Jesus, so that they may destroy him (so far as it lies in themselves) and have Barabbas set free; for the crowds believe their chiefs and priests. And for the most part the governor indeed said to the people: Which of the two do you wish that I release to you?, but the crowds — as being true crowds and many, who walk the "broad way that leads to destruction" — asked that Barabbas be released, wishing to have him set free for themselves.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But the populace, like wild beasts that rage the open plains, would have Barabbas released to them. For this people had seditions, murders, robberies, practised by some of their own nation in act, and nourished by all of them who believe not in Jesus, inwardly in their mind. Where Jesus is not, there are strifes and fightings; where He is, there is peace and all good things. All those who are like the Jews either in doctrine or life desire Barabbas to be loosed to them; for whoso does evil, Barabbas is loosed in his body, and Jesus bound; but he that does good has Christ loosed, and Barabbas bound. Pilate sought to strike them with shame for so great injustice, What shall I do then with Jesus that is called Christ? And not that only, but desiring to fill up the measure of their guilt. But neither do they blush that Pilate confessed Jesus to be the Christ, nor set any bounds to their impiety, They all say unto him, Let him be crucified. Thus they multiplied the sum of their wickedness, not only asking the life of a murderer, but the death of a righteous man, and that the shameful death of the cross.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Pilate says to them: What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ? They all say: Let him be crucified, and so on.

Wishing to strike into them shame at so great a wickedness, Pilate says to them: What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ, and not only this but also wishing to take the full measure of their impiety. But they, neither blushing at the fact that Pilate confessed Jesus to be Christ nor keeping any limit in their impiety, all said: Let him be crucified. And indeed, if they had asked that Barabbas be released, but had not on the contrary also demanded Christ for the cross — that is, if they had asked that Barabbas be acquitted, but had not asked that this man be crucified but had left him in Pilate's power, so that he might do with him what he willed — it would still have been of great impiety, that, leaving aside the just man, they had asked for a murderer. But as it is, they multiplied the measure of their impiety, not only demanding a murderer for life, but also the just man for death, and for the most shameful death of the cross. Yet still continuing in that very purpose by which he wished to confound them, so that at least, being confounded, they might come to the choosing of the just man (even if not from the judgment of the heart), he says to them: For what evil has he done? Having nothing to answer against this, they cried out the more, not laying aside but increasing their anger, their fury, their blasphemy, and said: Let him be crucified.

But Pilate, seeing that he was accomplishing nothing, made use of a Jewish custom, wishing to appease them concerning Christ's innocence not only by words but even by the deed itself, if they were willing, but if they were unwilling, to condemn — doing this not according to any custom of the Romans; for he took water in the sight of all, and washing his hands he said: I am innocent of the blood of this just man; see you to it. And he indeed washed himself, but they not only refused to cleanse themselves of Christ's blood, but even took it upon themselves, saying: His blood be upon us, and upon our children. On account of this they were made guilty not only in the blood of the prophets, but, filling up the measure of their fathers, they were made guilty also in the blood of Christ, so that they might hear God saying to them: When you stretch out your hands to me, I will turn away my eyes from you; for your hands are full of blood." Therefore the blood of Jesus was brought not only upon those who were then alive, but also upon all the generations of the Jews following afterward, even to the consummation. Therefore until now their house is left to them desolate. But Pilate, forgetting his own good words, by which he had begun to defend the innocence of Christ, turning aside to evil, not only delivered up Jesus, but even delivered him up scourged with whips, that they might crucify him.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Then the soldiers of the governor took Jesus into the praetorium and gathered to him the whole cohort, and clothed him with a scarlet chlamys and put purple around him, and placed a crown of thorns upon his head and a reed in his right hand, and kneeling down they mocked him, saying: Hail, King of the Jews.

It is likely that (in the beginnings of the then newly established Roman empire) the soldiers, not yet keeping the fitting order of discipline, did to the Savior — beyond the custom of the discipline that now exists — this: when, receiving him into the praetorium, they gathered the whole cohort and did what they are said to have done, making Jesus their sport, because he had been named King of the Jews. But I for my part think the soldiers did this while there worked within them the invisible kings and princes of this world, who "stood by and came together in one against the Lord and against his Christ", so that that mockery of theirs may be seen to have been rather theirs than men's — and of those who in that dispensation did not know the wisdom of God, "for if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty". Therefore that cohort was a mystery of some malignant host.

And they stripped him of his garments, which he had from above, the seamless tunic and the robe (for such does John describe his garments to be), and they clothed him (mocking him on account of his royal name) with a scarlet chlamys, not understanding what they do:

for that scarlet chlamys was a mystery of the scarlet sign which is written of in Joshua son of Nun, which that Rahab had for her salvation, and in Genesis, which was done upon one of the sons of Tamar at the hand of the one being born, that the scarlet should be bound as a sign of the future passion of Christ. Therefore now also the Lord, taking upon himself the scarlet chlamys, took upon himself the blood of the world,

and in that thorny crown he took upon himself the thorns of our sins woven into his head.

And concerning the chlamys it is written that they again stripped him of the scarlet chlamys, but concerning the thorny crown the evangelists wrote nothing of the sort, on account of which they wished us to seek out the outcome of the matter concerning the thorny crown, once placed on and never taken off. I therefore judge that that thorny crown was consumed from the head of Jesus, so that our old thorns are now no more, after Jesus once took them away from us upon his venerable head.

But if it is fitting to say something also about the reed which they placed in his right hand, we set forth a reasoning of this kind. That reed, then, was a mystery of a vain and fragile scepter, upon which we all leaned before we believed, a malignant scepter; for we trusted in the reed rod of Egypt or of Babylon or of whatever kingdom contrary against the kingdom of God.

And he took that reed and the rod of the fragile kingdom out of our hands, that he might triumph over it and crush it on the wood of the cross. And in place of that former reed, upon which we formerly reclined, he gave us the scepter of the heavenly kingdom

and the rod of which it is written: "the rod of equity is the rod of thy kingdom"; or a rod which may chastise those who have need of chastisement, of which the apostle says: "what will you? shall I come to you with a rod?" He gave us also a staff, that we might celebrate the Passover according to what is written: "let your staffs be in your hands", so that we might celebrate the Passover laying aside the reed rod which we had before we celebrated the Lord's Passover. But they strike with this fragile and vain reed the venerable head of Jesus, since that contrary kingdom also always reviles and beats God the Father — the head of the Lord the Savior. And in all these things the only-begotten power was not harmed, just as it also suffered nothing, though made "a curse for us", when by nature it was a blessing; but, being a blessing, it consumed and dissolved and dispersed every human curse.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Or, The reed was a mystery signifying that before we believed we trusted in that reed of Egypt, or Babylon, or of some other kingdom opposed to God, which He took that He might triumph over it with the wood of the cross. With this reed they smite the head of Christ, because this kingdom ever beats against God the Father, who is the head of the Saviour.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Of the cloak it is mentioned that they took it off Him, but of the crown of thorns the Evangelists have not spoken, so that there are now no longer those ancient thorns of ours, since Jesus has taken them from us upon His revered head.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Or, as they went out, they laid hold of Simon, but when they drew near to the place in which they would crucify Him, they laid the cross upon Him that He might bear it. Simon obtained not this office by chance, but was brought to the spot by God's providence, that he might be found worthy of mention in the Scriptures of the Gospel, and of the ministry of the cross of Christ. And it was not only meet that the Saviour should carry His cross, but meet also that we should take part therein, filling a carriage so beneficial to us, ἀγγαρεία. Yet would it not have so profited us to take it on us, as we have profited by His taking it upon Himself.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
And as they went out, they found a man of Cyrene named Simon; him they compelled to take up his cross.

For just as, according to the three evangelists, Jesus is tempted by the devil, but according to John (who made his discourse concern his spiritual nature) he is not tempted — for "the truth and the life" and "the resurrection" and "the true light" is not tempted, but he was tempted according to the man whom the only-begotten God had taken up — so according to John indeed the Savior, when those who had seized him laid it upon him, "bearing his own cross went out to the place which is called the place of Calvary", but according to the rest he does not bear it for himself.

For those who were leading him away to be crucified, as they went out, found a certain man of Cyrene, named Simon, whom they compelled to take up the cross of Christ. But it was fitting not only for the Savior to take up his own cross, but it was fitting also for us to bear it, fulfilling the compulsion that is salutary for us. Nor, again, would we have been to be profited so much by taking up his cross, as we are now profited by his cross, when he himself takes it up for himself and bears it.

But you will ask whether according to the text both things happened and the evangelists are not discordant with one another, and which of them happened first: that is, whether those who seized Jesus for crucifixion and laid the cross upon him, so that "bearing it" he might go out into the place of Calvary, did this first, before they compelled Simon of Cyrene — or whether, once they had gone out, they compelled Simon, but when they had come to the place in which they were going to hang him, they themselves placed the cross upon him, so that he himself might bear it.
